html:
The Hittites were a Bronze Age people of central Anatolia, in today's Turkey, who spoke the oldest written Indo-European language. On the map they appear from 2000 to 700 BCE.

From their capital Hattusa they built the Hittite kingdom from about 1650 BCE. In 1595 BCE their king Mursili I raided down the Euphrates and sacked Babylon, ending the Old Babylonian kingdom. At its height in the 1300s and 1200s BCE the empire stretched into Syria and was a rival of Egypt. At the Battle of Kadesh in 1274 BCE the Hittites fought Ramesses II to a draw, and the two powers later signed one of the earliest known peace treaties. Their laws survive on clay tablets.

The empire fell around 1180 BCE in the Late Bronze Age collapse, and Hattusa was abandoned. The map keeps the name after that for the small "Neo-Hittite" kingdoms of southern Anatolia and northern Syria, such as Carchemish, which kept Hittite royal names and art until Assyria absorbed them in the 700s BCE.
